newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia defiant over car policy challenges.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia defiant over car policy challenges.

text.p: Indonesia remained defiant on Friday despite formal complaints from the United States, Japan and the European Union to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) over a controversial national car policy.

Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told a news conference in Jakarta on Friday the U.S. would lodge a complaint with the WTO and in Tokyo a spokesman for the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) said Japan had complained to the Geneva-based trade organisation.
Along with the EU, which said on Thursday it would launch a formal complaint, they say Indonesia's national car plan violates international trade rules.

The policy announced earlier this year gives 100 percent tariff and luxury tax exemptions for three years to a company controlled by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra if the firm can meet local content requirements.
But despite the opposition to the Jakarta policy, Indonesian Industry and Trade Minister Tunky Ariwibowo emerged defiant after a meeting with President Suharto on Friday.
"Indonesia will not change its car policy," he said.
"We have a policy and we will implement it and we will not change it on principle," Ariwibowo told reporters.
Lang said the United States in the past few days had "identified the national car policy as a problem".
"We are going to the use the WTO, not domestic trade laws," he said.
MITI Minister Shunpei Tsukahara earlier told reporters Japan had decided to complain to the WTO after asking Indonesia three times to make the car plan conform with trade rules.
Ariwibowo played down the dispute saying differences among WTO members were "normal", adding that the EU had already said it wanted to have consultations with Indonesia over the car policy.
"We are preparing to have consultations with the EU," he said.
Ariwibowo said he was not worried about retaliation.
"It could not be (possible) as we are members of the WTO and there are procedures for members of the WTO," he said.

The company controlled by Hutomo Mandala Putra, PT Timor Putra Nasional, this week began selling its fully imported Timor sedans, made by joint venture partner Kia Motors 67500.SK of South Korea. It plans to begin assembly of the vehicles in March next year before starting full production in 1998.
It must raise local content to 60 percent within three years but has been allowed to import a batch of cars from South Korea duty free, the first of which arrived in Indonesia last month.
Tokyo claims the special tax breaks violate WTO rules and puts rival manufacturers at a disadvantage.

Japanese carmakers, which enjoy a 95 percent share of the Indonesian vehicle market through joint-venture assembly and licensing arrangements with local firms, view the national car project as a threat.
With its tax-free status the car is half the price of some of its Japanese-made competitors.
PT Timor said on Thursday it had orders for 8,500 cars and planned to sell up to 50,000 cars by July next year. The company has set a target of 200,000 cars a year by the end of the decade.
